newsitem.title: INDIA: New Indian PM keeps most of Deve Gowda's cabinet.
newsitem.headline: New Indian PM keeps most of Deve Gowda's cabinet.

text.p: Inder Kumar Gujral was sworn in on Monday as India's 12th prime minister at the head of a cabinet little changed from that of his ousted predecessor but without its economic czar, P. Chidambaram.
Gujral, a 77-year-old scholar with deep experience in foreign affairs, took the oath of office in English before President Shankar Dayal Sharma in the ornate sandstone presidential palace.
After pronouncing the oath, Gujral, wearing a blue-grey suit, bowed with clasped hands to the dignitaries attending the solemn ceremony.

Gujral then shook hands with Congress party president Sitaram Kesri, who provoked the downfall of outgoing prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda by withdrawing his party's vital support for the United Front coalition government on March 30.

Congress, fearing snap polls and satisfied that Deve Gowda had been replaced, has pledged to support Gujral in a vote of confidence set for 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) on Tuesday in the lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha.
Gujral retained all but five ministers from Deve Gowda's cabinet, presidential aides said.
Significantly, outgoing finance minister P. Chidambaram was not included among the 34 ministers who were sworn in one-by-one after Gujral.

Chidambaram's regional Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) party decided on Saturday not to join Gujral's government after the United Front coalition passed over its leader, G.K. Moopanar, and chose Gujral instead as its leader.
Three other TMC members and a member of Gujral's Janata Dal party also did not return as government ministers.
Gujral, who was external affairs minister during Deve Gowda's 10-month-old government, told reporters that he had kept both the foreign and finance portfolios to himself.
Politicians said Gujral was trying to woo Chidambaram, a favourite of financial markets because of his commitment to economic reforms, to return to the government.
Gujral's appointment followed three weeks of political upheaval triggered by Congress's shock decision to withdraw its support.
Question marks still lingered over the intentions of the TMC and the future of the federal budget for 1997/98 (April-March).
Chidambaram's TMC, piqued at being passed over during wrangling over a successor to Deve Gowda, said it would remain out of the government but support it in parliament.
The goateed Gujral was assured victory in Tuesday's confidence vote as he was backed by the United Front's 178 lawmakers as well as by Congress's 140 in the 542-member lower house.
